result.overall: The Court dismissed Ms. Ambroise's application for judicial review, finding the RAD's IFA analysis reasonable and no breach of procedural fairness, as she had a fair opportunity to address the IFA issue.

themes.name: Internal Flight Alternative (IFA) Analysis
themes.summary: The Court considered whether the RAD reasonably found Cap-Haïtien to be a viable IFA for Ms. Ambroise, addressing both risk of persecution and reasonableness of relocation.

themes.name: Risk of Persecution and State Protection
themes.summary: The Court addressed whether the RAD erred by not analyzing state protection and whether Ms. Ambroise faced a serious possibility of persecution as a woman in Haiti.

themes.name: Procedural Fairness
themes.summary: The Court examined whether the RPD breached procedural fairness by not raising the IFA at the outset of the hearing and whether Ms. Ambroise had a fair opportunity to respond.

themes.name: Standard of Review
themes.summary: The Court clarified the applicable standards of review for the IFA merits (reasonableness) and procedural fairness (correctness/fairness).

themes.name: Assessment of Evidence and Personal Circumstances
themes.summary: The Court considered whether the RAD properly assessed the documentary evidence and Ms. Ambroise's personal circumstances, including employment prospects and family ties in Cap-Haïtien.

themes.name: Case Law on Gender-Based Violence and IFA Reasonableness
themes.summary: The Court discussed relevant case law on gender-based violence, the need for individualized risk assessment, and when lack of employment makes an IFA unreasonable.

arguments.quote: Ms. Ambroise alleges that the RAD erred in its analysis of the two-prong IFA test.
arguments.claim: The RAD failed to properly apply the two-prong IFA test, including risk of persecution and reasonableness of relocation.
arguments.outcome_note: Court found the RAD's analysis reasonable on both prongs.

arguments.quote: the RAD failed to recognize that state protection for women is lacking throughout Haiti
arguments.claim: The RAD erred by not analyzing the lack of state protection for women in Haiti before concluding there was a viable IFA.
arguments.outcome_note: Court held state protection analysis not required if no serious possibility of persecution established.

arguments.quote: the IFA would be unreasonable for her because she would face a serious risk of sexual violence and would be unable to obtain employment in her profession
arguments.claim: The IFA in Cap-Haïtien is unreasonable due to risk of sexual violence and inability to work as a nurse.
arguments.outcome_note: Court found RAD's conclusion reasonable; lack of employment does not make IFA unreasonable except in exceptional cases.

arguments.quote: the RAD’s decision breached procedural fairness because the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) member failed to state at the outset of the hearing that an IFA would be raised.
arguments.claim: Procedural fairness was breached because the IFA was not raised at the outset of the RPD hearing.
arguments.outcome_note: Court found Ms. Ambroise had a fair opportunity to respond to the IFA issue during the hearing.
arguments.gap: did not seek leave to present further evidence or submissions after hearing; did not request RAD to allow further evidence under s. 110(4) IRPA

arguments.quote: the RAD considered there to be no basis to Ms. Ambroise’s allegations that her two attackers had the ability and motivation to find her wherever she might be.
arguments.claim: Ms. Ambroise failed to establish a serious possibility of persecution from her attackers in Cap-Haïtien.

arguments.quote: the RAD concluded that Ms. Ambroise failed to establish that it would be unreasonable to relocate to Cap-Haïtien.
arguments.claim: Ms. Ambroise failed to show that relocating to Cap-Haïtien would be unreasonable under the second prong of the IFA test.

arguments.quote: the RAD concluded that a refugee protection claim cannot be based solely on reports of the situation in the country.
arguments.claim: General country reports alone are insufficient to establish a serious possibility of persecution; personal circumstances must be considered.

holdings.quote: I am of the opinion that the RAD’s decision is reasonable.
holdings.statement: The RAD's decision regarding the IFA and risk of persecution was reasonable.

holdings.quote: the RAD’s analysis of the danger or risk that Ms. Ambroise would face in the identified IFA within the meaning of section 97 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act...was reasonable
holdings.statement: The RAD reasonably analyzed the risk Ms. Ambroise would face in Cap-Haïtien under section 97 IRPA.

holdings.quote: the RAD’s conclusion that there was no “serious possibility” that Ms. Ambroise would face persecution as a Haitian woman in the IFA within the meaning of section 96 were reasonable
holdings.statement: The RAD reasonably concluded there was no serious possibility of persecution for Ms. Ambroise in Cap-Haïtien under section 96 IRPA.

holdings.quote: it was reasonable for the RAD to conclude that Ms. Ambroise failed to meet the high threshold for establishing that the identified IFA is unreasonable.
holdings.statement: The RAD reasonably found Ms. Ambroise did not meet the high threshold to show the IFA was unreasonable.

holdings.quote: there was no breach of procedural fairness.
holdings.statement: There was no breach of procedural fairness in how the IFA was raised at the RPD hearing.

holdings.quote: the application for judicial review is dismissed.
holdings.statement: The application for judicial review is dismissed.

holdings.quote: the standard that applies to the second issue is the standard that applies to issues of procedural fairness, whether it be called the correctness standard or simply the fairness standard.
holdings.statement: Procedural fairness issues are reviewed on the correctness/fairness standard.

holdings.quote: the issue of an IFA “is always an issue in a refugee hearing”
holdings.statement: The IFA is always an issue in a refugee hearing, but claimants must be warned if it will be raised.

holdings.quote: procedural fairness does not require that an IFA be raised at the outset of the hearing, although it is preferable to do so as early as possible
holdings.statement: Procedural fairness is satisfied if the claimant has a fair opportunity to respond to the IFA, even if raised during the hearing.

holdings.quote: Ms. Ambroise had the opportunity at the hearing to present her case regarding the IFA
holdings.statement: Ms. Ambroise had a reasonable opportunity to address the IFA at the hearing.

rebuttals.point: The RAD erred by not analyzing state protection for women in Haiti before concluding there was a viable IFA.
rebuttals.court_answer: State protection analysis is not required if no serious possibility of persecution is established.

rebuttals.quote: I do not find it unreasonable for the RAD to conclude that Ms. Ambroise failed to establish, on a balance of probabilities, that she would face a risk of persecution or danger from those men in Cap-Haïtien.
rebuttals.point: The RAD unreasonably found Ms. Ambroise's attackers would not pursue her in Cap-Haïtien.
rebuttals.court_answer: There was no evidence her attackers had the ability or interest to pursue her; unlike in Dominguez Bando, there was no pursuit elsewhere.

rebuttals.quote: I cannot conclude that there was a breach of procedural fairness.
rebuttals.point: Procedural fairness was breached because the IFA was not raised at the outset of the RPD hearing.
rebuttals.court_answer: Ms. Ambroise had a fair opportunity to respond to the IFA during the hearing and did not seek to present further evidence.

authorities.quote: Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration) v Vavilov, 2019 SCC 65
authorities.why: Sets out the reasonableness standard for reviewing administrative decisions.
Clarifies when state protection analysis is required in refugee claims.

authorities.quote: Thirunavukkarasu v Canada (Minister of Employment and Immigration), [1994] 1 FC 589 (CA)
authorities.why: Sets out the IFA test and reasonableness threshold.

authorities.quote: Dezameau v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2010 FC 559
authorities.why: Court found the RAD did not make the error described in Dezameau.

authorities.quote: Josile v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2011 FC 39
authorities.why: Court found the RAD properly considered personal circumstances, unlike in Josile.

authorities.quote: Jean v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2019 FC 242
authorities.why: Cited for the principle that country reports alone are insufficient for a refugee claim.

authorities.quote: Alkhoury v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2020 FC 153
authorities.why: Clarifies procedural fairness requirements for IFA notice.

authorities.quote: Tariq v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2017 FC 1017
authorities.why: Addresses standard of review and procedural fairness for IFA notice.

authorities.quote: Mchedlishvilli v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2010 FC 630
authorities.why: States that inability to find employment may or may not make IFA unreasonable.

authorities.quote: Mora Alcca v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2020 FC 236
authorities.why: Confirms that only in exceptional circumstances does lack of employment make IFA unreasonable.

left_open.quote: the applicable standard does not affect the outcome in any event, given my conclusion on this issue.
left_open.issue: Whether the procedural fairness standard is called correctness or fairness standard.
left_open.reason: Court found the outcome would be the same regardless of terminology.
